evidence.source: CUHK Humanum 漢語多功能字庫
evidence.text: Oracle-bone 水 uses a central stroke for flowing water and side dots for droplets, with varying dot counts. As a component it can be reduced to droplets. Bronze and Warring States forms continue the water picture.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 水

evidence.field: 形義通解; 字形; 甲骨文用例; 金文用例
evidence.text: The entry describes 水 as a picture of flowing water: oracle forms vary in the number of strokes, with a central stroke for the current and side dots for droplets; component forms may reduce the current to drops. Bronze forms retain the flowing-water picture, and Warring States forms follow the bronze forms. The page reports Shang oracle usage for water/flooding in 合集 10150 (“其㞢(有)大水”), a ritual use in 合集 14407, and a disputed verbal use in 合集 23532 (“今日王其水𡨦(寢)”). A separate graph-borrowing use is reported on a bronze inscription, where 水 is read as 乞 ‘request’. These are reported examples in the database; inscription images were not inspected here.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 水

evidence.text: The entry quotes the Shuowen explanation “水，準也。北方之行。象眾水並流，中有微陽之气也。凡水之屬皆从水” and explains that its north/five-phase and yin-yang account reflects Han-era cosmology; it treats “水，準也” as phonetic glossing, not the graph’s original pictorial analysis. The database gives 水本義 as water and reports later 水準 as a compound for a leveling instrument, then an extended sense of a standard or level. It does not provide dated attestations for these later stages.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 水

evidence.field: 形義通解; 字形; 甲骨文用例; 金文用例
evidence.text: The entry analyzes 水 as a picture of flowing water: oracle forms vary in detail, with a central stroke for the current and side dots for droplets; component forms may reduce the current to drops. Bronze forms retain the flowing-water picture, and the entry says Warring States forms continue the bronze tradition. It reports Shang oracle use for water/flooding in 合集 10150, “其㞢(有)大水,” and another oracle use as a sacrificial name in 合集 14407. It also reports a disputed verbal use in 合集 23532 (“今日王其水𡨦(寢)”), with interpretations involving leveling ground with water or washing a temple. Bronze 水 is reported borrowed for 乞 ‘request’ in 沈子簋. These are the database’s reported readings and analyses; the record does not establish the disputed verb’s semantic connection to the noun.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 水

evidence.source: 說文解字在線查詢 Shuowen.org
evidence.field: 水 entry; Shuowen text and Duan Yucai commentary
evidence.text: The page transcribes the Shuowen entry: 水，凖也。北方之行。象眾水並流，中有微陽之气也。凡水之屬皆从水。This is a Han-era account combining a gloss with cosmological interpretation. CUHK’s palaeographic discussion instead treats the character’s graph as picturing flowing water and interprets “水，準也” as phonetic glossing; therefore the Shuowen passage is evidence for a historical explanation, not by itself proof of the graph’s original formation.
evidence.title: 說文解字「水」

evidence.text: The inspected file page identifies 水-oracle.svg as a vector depiction of 水 in Shang oracle-script style. It lists Sinica Database, Chinese Etymology, and CUHK among character-form sources, points to the source image as 43.E7BE and notes “甲903 合34165.” The drawing is a modern vector representation, not an artifact photograph. The page offers the original image at https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/75/%E6%B0%B4-oracle.svg and states CC0 1.0/public-domain reuse.

gaps: No individual oracle-bone, bronze, or manuscript glyph image was visually inspected; the CUHK account is a textual description.
The earliest cited attestation in this inspected source is Shang oracle-bone material, but the page does not date each shell inscription individually. It reports 合集 identifiers and example readings.

The alleged verbal “water” use in 合集 23532 is disputed in the CUHK account; its alternatives are leveling land with water or washing a temple. The semantic link to the ordinary noun is not established here.
The bronze use of 水 as a phonetic loan for 乞 is reported separately from the pictorial origin; no reconstruction comparison was established in the accessible sources.
No sound component occurs in the character 水 itself. Its graphic analysis is pictographic; modern readings and Old Chinese reconstructions concern the spoken word, not a phonetic subcomponent.

The local Baxter–Sagart table has a 水 row (*s.turʔ; MC sywijX), but this session did not inspect an accessible official character-specific online row. The proposed comparative Austroasiatic/Sino-Tibetan analyses in the dossier remain unresolved and were not independently investigated in the bounded searches.
Current Mandarin shuǐ is present in both local Unihan sources, but the exact official Unicode Unihan URL was inaccessible, so the required official click-through verification is missing.
No local reading comparison with another component is needed because 水 has no proposed phonetic component. The local Unihan_Readings.txt and Baxter–Sagart files were present and 水 rows were checked.
The cited CUHK page states later 水準 senses but supplies no dated attestations for the measurement sense or its later abstract extension.

The earliest cited evidence in the inspected character-specific source is Shang oracle-bone material, but its 合集 examples are not individually dated there; a narrower date for each attestation remains unverified.
The relationship, if any, between the ordinary water noun and the disputed oracle-bone verbal use in 合集 23532 is unresolved; the source gives competing interpretations.
The bronze graph-loan reading 水 for 乞 is reported by CUHK, but this research did not independently establish the two words’ historical phonological match.
The stages of the 水準 leveling-instrument sense and its abstract extension are described without dated attestations in the inspected source.

No sound component or independently established sound component role applies to 水. Comparative etymologies and competing Old Chinese reconstructions in the supplied dossier were not independently checked in this bounded search.

The proposed glyphs are modern vector redrawings of historical script forms, not photographs of ancient artifacts. The source databases are named by the Commons pages, but the underlying inscription artifacts were not independently inspected here.

Commons supplied exact original SVG links on inspected description pages; the web reader could not render SVG responses. No visual inspection of their pixels was performed. The Xiaoxuetang 水 query record was not successfully opened, so no Xiaoxuetang image is proposed.
